stops.name: York House, the Strand — birth
stops.campa: Francis Bacon is born at York House on the Strand, London seat of his father Sir Nicholas Bacon, Lord Keeper of the Great Seal to Elizabeth I. His mother, Anne Cooke Bacon, a scholar of Greek and a fierce reforming Protestant, will shape his mind before any tutor does. He is the youngest of Nicholas's second family, a small grave child in a household already at the hinge of the state: the Great Seal kept upstairs, statesmen at the table below. Law, learning, and the court share one roof over his cradle.

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge — entrance
stops.campa: At not quite twelve years old, Francis and his elder brother Anthony go up together to Trinity College, Cambridge, put under the tutelage of the Master, John Whitgift, future Archbishop of Canterbury. Francis is the youngest member of the college. He works with a gravity beyond his years and begins forming, in these rooms, the conviction he will carry his whole life: that the learning of the schools, built on Aristotle at second and third hand, is a barren inheritance, endlessly argued and never tested against nature herself.

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge — the verdict against Aristotle
stops.campa: Before he leaves Cambridge at not yet fifteen, Bacon arrives, so his first biographer and chaplain William Rawley will record, at a judgment against the philosopher the whole university still swears by. He conceives a dislike of Aristotle's philosophy, Rawley writes, not for the worthlessness of the author but for the unfruitfulness of the way: a philosophy strong for disputations, barren of works for the benefit of man's life. It is the seed of everything after: the Advancement, the Novum Organum, a learning meant to bear fruit, not argument.
stops.quote: the unfruitfulness of the way; being a philosophy... only strong for disputations and contentions, but barren of the production of works for the benefit of the life of man
stops.quote_source: William Rawley, Life of the Honourable Author (1657 preface to Resuscitatio), recounting Bacon's own account

stops.name: Gray's Inn — admission
stops.campa: Back in London, Francis is admitted to Gray's Inn on the same day as his brother Anthony, entered de societate magistrorum on the books of the Inn of Court where his father kept chambers before him. He is meant for the law, the family trade, though his ambitions already reach further: not merely to plead causes but to reform the whole estate of knowledge. Within three months the Inn will lend him out again, across the Channel, into the household of a newly appointed ambassador to France.

stops.name: Paris — into the household of Sir Amias Paulet
stops.campa: In September, Queen Elizabeth having newly knighted Sir Amias Paulet and sent him as ambassador to the French court, Francis Bacon crosses to Paris in his train, put under his charge to learn the business of embassies. He carries dispatches to Walsingham, Burghley, Leicester, and the Queen herself, and begins the double education of a diplomat's clerk: the cipher and the code on one hand, the manners of princes on the other. Paris in these years is a court of plots and factions, the massacre of Saint Bartholomew still raw in memory.

stops.name: Poitiers and the itinerant French court — civil law, and a cipher conceived
stops.campa: The embassy is itinerant, and Bacon follows the French court through its round of chateaux, Fontainebleau, Blois, Tours, Poitiers, Chenonceaux, carrying letters and watching the machinery of a foreign state at close range. At Poitiers he takes up civil law, the Roman-descended law of the continent, sharpening the comparative eye he will later turn on England's own courts. And here, not yet eighteen, he conceives the device that will outlast every office he ever holds: a cipher hiding one letter inside the shape of five, so any text at all may carry a second, secret text within it.

stops.name: Paris — the dream of Gorhambury in black mortar, and the father's death
stops.campa: Preparing to travel on into Italy, Bacon dreams one February night that Gorhambury, his father's house, stands plastered all over in black mortar. A fortnight later the news reaches Paris: on the twentieth, Sir Nicholas Bacon has died suddenly at York House, before completing the estate he meant to settle on his youngest son. Francis, not yet eighteen, abandons the Italian journey and sails home to a diminished inheritance, the law now not a choice but a necessity.

stops.name: Gray's Inn — the return, and the call to the law
stops.campa: Home in a country he has not lived in for three years, Bacon takes up residence at Gray's Inn and commits himself to the profession his father followed to the highest office in the land. The Continental polish, the civil law, the taste for cipher and secret method, all of it now bends toward the English bar, where a second son with no great fortune must make his own way by wit and patronage. He will be called to the bar within a few years, but the Essex years, not the law alone, will make him.

stops.name: Westminster — first seat in Parliament, for Bossiney
stops.campa: Bacon takes his first seat in the House of Commons, elected for the Cornish borough of Bossiney, beginning a parliamentary career that will run nearly four decades under three sovereigns. He is not yet twenty. Already he studies the House as he studies nature: a mechanism whose working parts, precedents and procedures, he means to master. He will sit for Melcombe, Taunton, Liverpool, and Middlesex in turn, gaining a reputation as one of the ablest speakers in England, admired even by those who distrust his ambition.

stops.name: Whitehall — the letter to Lord Burghley: 'all knowledge my province'
stops.campa: To his uncle by marriage, Lord Burghley, on whose favor his early career still depends, Bacon writes the letter that will be quoted longer than any office he ever holds. He confesses moderate ambitions in the state and vast ones in the mind: he means to purge the whole estate of learning of its two plagues, frivolous disputation and blind, credulous experiment, and bring in grounded, fruitful knowledge in their place. It is a young man's manifesto for the work of his whole life, decades before the Novum Organum gives it method.
stops.quote: I have taken all knowledge to be my province; and if I could purge it of two sorts of rovers, whereof the one with frivolous disputations, confutations, and verbosities, the other with blind experiments and auricular traditions and impostures, hath committed so many spoils, I hope I should bring in industrious observations, grounded conclusions, and profitable inventions and discoveries; the best state of that province.

stops.name: Gray's Inn — the Gesta Grayorum, six speeches for the Prince of Purpoole
stops.campa: In the Christmas revels of Gray's Inn, the mock court of the Prince of Purpoole, Bacon writes six speeches of counsel for the Prince's councillors, urging in turn the study of philosophy, of arms, of eternal fame, of virtue, of the tillage of the mind, and of pastimes and sports: a masque of ambition disguised as entertainment. The same nights see the first recorded performance of a play called The Comedy of Errors in the crowded, overheated hall. Bacon works the revel like everything else: as an exercise in the government of minds.

stops.name: Twickenham Park — Essex's gift
stops.campa: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, unable to win Bacon the Attorney's or Solicitor's place he has lobbied for, gives his friend and counselor instead the property at Twickenham Park, a riverside house and grounds upstream of London, in compensation for a service patronage alone could not reward. Bacon keeps it for years, walking the gardens between law terms, testing early thoughts on soils and orchards there, and sells it in the end for eighteen hundred pounds. It is the clearest sign yet of how much the two men owe each other, and of how little that debt will finally protect either of them.
